To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

in a cohort of adults who developed cancer, diabetes was associated, in adjusted analyses, with a higher risk for incident cancer (1.22 [0.98–153]), cancer mortality (1,36 [1.0021.81]), cancer case fatality in those who developed cancer (1.34 (1.002– 1.79]) as well as all cause mortality (1.60 [1.29 –2.01]) in those who developed diabetes.
in this cohort, diabetes was associated, in people with incident cancer, with a higher risk for mortality and cancer case fatality than for incident cancer.

treated diabetes is associated with an increased risk of incident cancer, cancer mortality, and cancer case fatality in adults, and that treated diabetes accounts for a larger proportion of cancer mortality and case fatality than cancer incidence.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the association of type 2 diabetes and the incidence and mortality of cancer.
the role of diabetes in the etiology and prognosis of cancer.
understanding the relationship between diabetes and cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
diabetes increases cancer incidence, cancer fatality, and all-cause death.
the association between diabetes and cancer is complex and that diabetes may influence cancer incidence, case fatality, and mortality in a variety of ways.

diabetes is associated with a greater risk of death from cancer, and this is due, at least in part, to the fact that diabetes is associated, at least in some instances, with an increased risk of cancer death.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
diabetes is an important factor to consider in cancer outcomes.
the diabetes-cancer association is complex and that the association of diabetes with cancer incidence is not as strong as its association with cancer mortality.
diabetes appears to be a risk factor for cancer case fatality.
The main takeaway from our work is that
diabetes is a risk factor for cancer outcomes.

, although diabetes is a risk factor for many types of cancer, it is a more important risk factor for cancer case fatality, cancer mortality, and all-cause cancer mortality than it is for the risk of incident cancer.
diabetes appears to have a greater impact on the outcomes of people who develop cancer than in preventing cancer in the first place.
